funFacts: 第一 is also ‘the best, number one’: 他是我们班第一 ‘he is top of our class’.
pitfalls: 一 keeps its first tone in ordinals: dì-yī, also before a fourth tone (第一次 dì-yī cì) — the spoken yí / yì of 一 does not apply.
subtleties: In a list of points, 第一, 第二 … mean ‘firstly, secondly …’.

pitfalls: Ordinals always use 二: 第二, never *第两 — even before a measure word (第二个).
subtleties: Months, weekdays and dates use the bare number: 二月 ‘February’, 星期二 ‘Tuesday’, 二号 ‘the 2nd’ — no 第.

funFacts: 四 sì ‘four’ sounds like 死 sǐ ‘to die’, so some buildings have no fourth floor.

subtleties: A rank is 第四名 (名 for places in a ranking); a day is 第四天 (天 counts itself).

etymology.text: 最 ‘most’ + 后 ‘behind, after’ (traditional 後): ‘the very last’ — a frozen superlative (S17).

funFacts: 最后 is a superlative frozen into a word: 最 ‘most’ (S17) + 后 ‘after’.
pitfalls: ‘Last week, last month’ (the previous one) is 上个星期, 上个月; 最后一个月 is ‘the final month’.
subtleties: As ‘last’ it comes before a number + measure word (最后一个, 最后两天); as ‘finally’ it opens the sentence or stands before the verb.

funFacts: The saying 好的开始是成功的一半 ‘a good start is half the success’ is the Chinese ‘well begun is half done’.
pitfalls: 一半 is a whole word and takes no measure word: 一半的苹果 / 苹果的一半; with a measure word use 半: 半个苹果.
subtleties: 一半 can be the subject or the object: 一半是你的 ‘half is yours’, 我吃了一半 ‘I ate half’.

etymology.text: Phono-semantic compound: phonetic 亥 + semantic 刂 ‘knife’ — first ‘to carve, to engrave’. As a unit of time Wiktionary gives two values: historically 1/100 of a day (14.4 minutes), today a quarter of an hour.

funFacts: Clock quarters: 一刻 15 minutes, 半 30 minutes (never *两刻), 三刻 45 minutes.
pitfalls: 刻 takes no measure word (一刻, not *一个刻); half an hour is 半, not *两刻.
The main meaning of the character is still ‘to carve, to engrave’ (刻字 ‘engrave characters’) — 刻 on a clock is a different use.
subtleties: In everyday speech 三点十五分 is as common as 三点一刻; 刻 sounds a little traditional.

etymology.text: 世 ‘generation, age’ + 纪 ‘record; era’ (as in 纪元 ‘era’).

funFacts: Centuries take no 第: 二十一世纪 is ‘the 21st century’ — the bare number works as an ordinal.
pitfalls: The 1900s as a century are 二十世纪; ‘the 1990s’ is 九十年代 (with 年代).
subtleties: 上个世纪 ‘last century’, 下个世纪 ‘next century’ — 上 / 下 as with months and weeks.

synonyms.nuance: shí nián: ten years — any stretch of ten years

etymology.text: 年 ‘year’ + 代 ‘generation, era’: ‘an era of years’.

funFacts: 八十年代 alone means the 1980s; with a century it can be any: 十九世纪八十年代 ‘the 1880s’.
pitfalls: ‘A decade’ as ten years of time is 十年 (我在北京住了十年); 年代 is a decade of the calendar (the ’80s) or an era.
subtleties: Big before small again: 二十世纪八十年代 ‘the 1980s’ — the century first, then the decade.

etymology.text: 周 ‘a full circle’ (traditional 週) + 年 ‘year’: ‘a full turn of the year’.

funFacts: Like 世纪, 周年 needs no 第: 十周年 is ‘the 10th anniversary’.
pitfalls: 周年 follows the number directly, without a measure word: 五周年 (not *五个周年).
subtleties: A child’s first birthday is 一周岁 ‘one full year of age’ — the same 周 ‘full circle’.
